KEY MESSAGE 1...As of 2:30 AM EDT...Current sfc analysis shows a 
1028 mb area of high pressure sitting over southeastern Canada,
with a frontal boundary draped to the W/SW of our region. With 
dew points in the 50s to 60s and fairly widespread cloud cover 
across the region, temperatures are running several degrees 
warmer than the previous few nights. Most areas are in the 60s,
except for the ADKs which have had more clearing that allowed 
temps to fall into the mid 50s. Temperatures only drop a couple 
more degrees from current levels between now and sunrise. Patchy
fog will also be possible anywhere breaks in the clouds develop
due to abundant low-level moisture. Mainly dry weather is 
expected through the rest of the night. 

Today, a weak area of low pressure will track from the Ohio Valley 
into our region along the frontal boundary in response to a weak 
upper impulse. This will actually help lift the boundary back north 
as a warm front, although the sfc front will only get to around the 
I-90 corridor. With ample moisture, there will be enough forcing 
(convergence along the boundary, mid-level warm advection/isentropic 
lift) for scattered to numerous showers to develop from mid-morning 
through this evening. Areas closer to I-84 may stay dry through 
early to mid afternoon. PWATs surge to 1.8-2.0" with warm cloud 
depths of around 12 kft, which could allow for some very heavy 
downpours. Some training of showers can't be ruled out with flow 
aloft relatively parallel to the frontal boundary. However, fast 
flow aloft and an overall lack of instability (MUCAPE <500 J/kg) 
should prevent any significant hydro issues, although some ponding 
of water in the typical urban, low-lying, and poor drainage areas 
will be possible. WPC has kept their marginal risk ERO just west of 
our region for today. A few rumbles of thunder can't be ruled out 
south of I-90, but lack of instability should also prevent any 
severe weather today. High temperatures were lowered a few degrees 
from the NBM for areas north of I-90 on the cool side of the 
boundary, but stayed near NBM highs (mid and uper 70s) for southern 
areas where it will take longer for showers to arrive. Showers come 
to and end from northwest to southeast this evening into early 
tonight, with total rainfall amounts ranging from 0.1 to 0.5". 


KEY MESSAGE 2...A strong cold front will track through the region 
tonight, pushing the showers off to our south and east. Ahead of the 
front, some patchy fog will be possible tonight due to lingering low-
level moisture. Tomorrow, much cooler and less humid weather is 
expected with breezy NW winds. We continued to bump up winds/gusts 
and lower dew points from the NBM Friday in the post-frontal 
airmass. Highs will be in the 60s (terrain) to 70s (valleys).

Friday night, a strong (1028+ mb) sfc high builds over southern 
Canada. While it won't be perfectly centered overhead, its proximity 
should allow for diminishing winds and favorable radiational cooling 
conditions Friday night. Lows will be in the 30s (terrain) to 40s 
(valleys). Some patchy frost can't be ruled out in the
sheltered areas of the ADKs Friday night. The sfc high slides 
overhead Saturday, resulting in a gorgeous early fall day. 
Morning sun will give way to increasing PM clouds with highs 
mainly in the 60s with low humidity.

Saturday night into Sunday, our next sfc low tracks over the region, 
bringing widespread rain/showers. Strengthening LLJ with a Gulf 
moisture connection will lead to PWATs surging to around 2 std dev 
above normal. Mid-level warm advection and the right entrance of the 
upper jet to our north will provide plenty of forcing for ascent. At 
this time, Sunday looks like a washout for most of the region. NBM 
seems to have caught on to the fact that temps will likely remain 
well below normal Sunday, but still doesn't look quite cool
enough. We therefore opted to lower temps a couple degrees from
the NBM, with 50s in the high terrain and low 60s for most 
valley areas. 

The forecast continues to trend drier for early next week, as 
guidance is coming into better agreement that another strong sfc 
high building into southern Canada will help push a frontal boundary 
back south of our region, keeping us dry and seasonably cool. 
However, some uncertainly remains in exactly how close this boundary 
will stall to the region and whether or not it may be able to lift 
back north towards the middle of next week, bringing with it 
additional rain chances. Will continue to monitor and refine this 
part of the forecast over the next several days.
